name: Arioch
title: Name borne by two biblical figures: the king of Ellasar and Nebuchadnezzar's chief of guards
lifespan: Patriarchal period (circa 20th century BC) and exile (circa 6th century BC)
summary: The name Arioch is linked in the Bible to two completely different figures, separated by well over a thousand years. The first is the king of Ellasar, who took part in a military coalition led by Kedorlaomer of Elam. This alliance waged war against five kings in the Valley of Siddim, won victory, and captured among others Abraham's nephew Lot — which triggered Abraham's bold military counterattack and liberation of the captives. The second Arioch served at King Nebuchadnezzar's court in Babylon as chief of the bodyguard. When the king demanded that the wise men not only interpret a dream but also recount its content — and no one could do it — Arioch received orders to execute them all. In this critical situation, Daniel approached Arioch with wisdom and caution, and Arioch explained the situation to him and later brought him before the king. Daniel's divinely inspired revelation of the dream saved the lives of the wise men and demonstrated God's sovereignty over the kingdoms of the earth.

keyEvents.title: Arioch as king of Ellasar in the war against the Valley of Siddim
keyEvents.description: Arioch, the king of Ellasar, allied with Kedorlaomer of Elam, Amraphel of Shinar, and Tidal of Goiim in the war against the five kings of the Valley of Siddim, including the kings of Sodom and Gomorrah.

keyEvents.title: The victory in the Valley of Siddim and the capture of Lot
keyEvents.description: Arioch and his allies defeated the kings of the Valley of Siddim and took away wealth and captives, including Lot, Abraham's nephew.

keyEvents.title: Abraham pursues and defeats Arioch and his allies
keyEvents.description: Abraham gathered 318 of his trained men, pursued Arioch and the allied kings to free his nephew Lot, and defeated them all the way to Hobah north of Damascus.

keyEvents.title: Arioch ordered the execution of the wise men in Babylon
keyEvents.description: In Daniel's time, Arioch, chief of King Nebuchadnezzar's bodyguard, was ordered to execute all the wise men in Babylon because none could tell the king what his dream contained or interpret it.

keyEvents.title: Daniel approaches Arioch
keyEvents.description: Daniel approached Arioch with wisdom and caution and asked about the reason for the king's harsh order. Arioch explained the situation to Daniel.

keyEvents.title: Arioch brings Daniel before Nebuchadnezzar
keyEvents.description: After God revealed the secret of the dream to Daniel in a night vision, Arioch brought him before King Nebuchadnezzar and presented him as one who could interpret the dream.

versions.summary: The name Arioch appears in two different contexts in the Bible. In Genesis, Arioch is the king of Ellasar who participated in the war against the kings of the Valley of Siddim. In the book of Daniel, Arioch is the chief of Nebuchadnezzar's bodyguard in Babylon, tasked with executing all the wise men, but instead brought Daniel before the king.
versions.title: The commander of the king of Ellasar and the chief of Nebuchadnezzar's bodyguard
versions.reason: [major] The title conflates two different individuals both named Arioch. The Arioch in Genesis 14 is himself a king (the king of Ellasar), not a military commander. The Arioch in Daniel 2 is the captain of the guard. The title should reflect that these are two distinct biblical figures sharing the same name.; [critical] Era is set to 'exile', but the Arioch from Genesis 14 lived during the patriarchal period (circa 2000 BC), whereas the Arioch in Daniel 2 lived during the exile. Since the profile covers both individuals, and the most well-known Arioch (the king of Ellasar) belongs to the patriarchal era, the era should either reflect the earliest occurrence or select the most prominent one. Alternatively, the profile should handle this explicitly. Given that both are included, 'patriarchs' should be used for the primary occurrence.; [major] The lifespan 'circa 600s BC' applies only to the Arioch in the book of Daniel. Arioch, the king of Ellasar, lived during the patriarchal period, around the 2000s BC. The lifespan should reflect both individuals.; [minor] The summary is good and explains both occurrences, but it should be made even clearer that these are likely two entirely different historical figures who share the same name, separated by over a thousand years.; [major] The roles 'warrior' and 'leader' are too general. Arioch in Genesis was a king, and Arioch in Daniel was the captain of the guard. These specific roles should be included.; [minor] In the event 'Daniel asks Arioch for delay' - it is actually not Daniel who asks Arioch for a delay. In Daniel 2:15, Daniel asks Arioch the reason for the order, and in verse 16, Daniel himself goes to the king and requests time. Arioch is an intermediary, but the extension of time is requested directly by Daniel from the king.

versions.summary: Arjok is a name that appears in two very different contexts in the Bible, likely borne by two entirely different historical figures separated by over a thousand years. In Genesis, Arjok is the king of Ellasar, one of four allied kings under the leadership of Kedorlaomer, who waged war against the kings of the Valley of Siddim and took Lot captive — an event that led to Abraham's military intervention. In the book of Daniel, Arjok is the commander of King Nebuchadnezzar's bodyguard in Babylon, tasked with executing all the wise men because none could interpret the king's dream. Arjok showed kindness toward Daniel and brought him before the king, resulting in the secret of the dream being revealed and the wise men being spared.
versions.title: Name borne by two biblical figures: the king of Ellasar and Nebuchadnezzar's chief of guards
versions.reason: [critical] The profile covers two different individuals from two completely different eras: the patriarchal period (Genesis 14) and the exile (Daniel 2). Assigning the era solely to 'patriarchs' is misleading. Since the profile treats both figures together, and the most prominent Arjok in the narrative context is the king of Ellasar from the patriarchal period, 'patriarchs' can be defended, but this should be clarified. Alternatively, 'exile' could have been chosen. Keep 'patriarchs' but note the issue.; [minor] Verse 15 is duplicated between event 4 and event 5. In event 5 (Daniel's appeal to Arjok), Daniel 2:15-16 is referenced, but verse 15 already belongs to event 4 (the order to kill the wise men). It is more precise to start event 5 from verse 16 to avoid overlap.; [minor] The summary closely resembles version 1 in structure and wording (starting with 'Arjok is a name that appears in two ... contexts in the Bible'). The instruction states that text should not resemble previous versions. A rewording is recommended.; [minor] The roles 'warrior' and 'military leader' partially overlap. For Arjok of Ellasar, 'king' and 'military leader' are appropriate, while 'warrior' is somewhat generic. Suggest keeping 'king', 'military leader', and 'captain of the guard', and replacing 'warrior' with 'court official' to better describe Arjok's role at the Babylonian court.; [minor] The description says 'execute all the wise men in Babylon' — this is correct according to Daniel 2:12-14, but it should be clarified that this was because none of the wise men could tell the king what the dream contained (not only interpret it, but also recount it).

The first is the king of Ellasar, who took part in a military coalition led by Kedorlaomer of Elam. This alliance waged war against five kings in the Valley of Siddim, won victory, and captured among others Abraham's nephew Lot — which triggered Abraham's bold military counterattack and liberation of the captives. Setting the era to 'patriarchs' covers only the first figure. Since this is a composite entry for two persons, one should choose the earliest period ('patriarchs'), but this should at least be clearly commented on. Alternatively, one could argue for 'exile' if the second figure is considered more important. Keep 'patriarchs' as the earliest, but mark the issue.; [minor] In the description it says that Daniel "went in to the king and asked for time" after Arioch explained the situation. The description is acceptable but slightly conflates who does what—in some readings, it is Daniel who goes directly to the king in verse 16, not via Arioch. footnotes.text: The name Arioch (Hebrew: אַרְיוֹךְ, Aryokh) may be derived from the Sumerian Eri-Aku, meaning 'servant of the moon god'. Some scholars have attempted to identify Arioch of Ellasar with Eri-Aku (Rim-Sin) of Larsa in Mesopotamia, but this identification is debated among modern researchers.

Ellasar, the city ruled by Arioch according to Genesis 14, has traditionally been identified with the Sumerian city of Larsa in southern Mesopotamia (modern Tell as-Senkereh in Iraq). Larsa was an important city-state during the Old Babylonian period and a center for the worship of the sun god Shamash.

The war described in Genesis 14 is the only text in the Pentateuch that places Abraham in a broader geopolitical context with named kings from Mesopotamia. The historicity of this account has been the subject of significant academic debate, but the mentioned names and political circumstances fit what is known about the Old Babylonian period.

The role of chief of the guards (Aramaic: רַב טַבָּחַיָּא, rav tabbachayya) literally means 'chief of the slaughterers'. This was a high-ranking military and administrative position at the Babylonian court, which also entailed responsibility for executions. A similar title is found in Akkadian in Neo-Babylonian administrative texts.

In rabbinic tradition, some scholars have seen a connection between the two Arioch figures as a literary device, where the name is reused to link the patriarchal narratives with the exile stories. In Midrash Bereshit Rabba, Arioch is mentioned in connection with Genesis 14 with various etymological explanations of the name.

The book of Daniel chapter 2 is written in Aramaic, not Hebrew, which reflects the Babylonian court environment. Arioch's name in this context thus appears in its Aramaic form, and the entire dialogue between Daniel and Arioch takes place within this linguistic framework.

The military coalition in Genesis 14, with four kings against five, reflects a pattern known from Mesopotamian war accounts where great powers demanded tribute from vassal states. Kedorlaomer's role as leader of the coalition aligns with Elam's historical dominance during parts of the Old Babylonian period.
